#252. Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1536 words)
General

Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Sumber: https://nulltx.com/enjin-matrixchain-votes-on-opengov-today-what-changes-for-enj-holders-on-november-16

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16.
  • Enjin's latest proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ.
  • According to recent reports, enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

It has been revealed that enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16. Here is how the 15 tracks, the 1,000 ENJ deposit and conviction voting work, and what the Relaychain vote shows.

Enjin's latest proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ. It's actually the cheap part.

According to recent reports, enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release. The referendum opened November 10. If it passes, the upgrade is targeted for November 16 at block #12,331,000, with the network moving from runtime 1.3.1 to 1.4.1. Enjin's Fort Canning announcement lays out the proposal, and the official changelog carries the technical detail.

The Relaychain has already made the jump. Referendum #16 approved its upgrade on October 28, and it went live on November 9. The Matrixchain vote is the second half of one upgrade, and it is the half that changes how Matrixchain makes decisions from then on.

Early coverage reported the schedule and the headline numbers: 15 tracks, 1,000 ENJ. The changelog and the governance portal show the mechanics behind them, and those mechanics change more than the headlines suggest.

Recent findings suggest that today, the Matrixchain runs its governance through the older Democracy, Council and Technical Committee pallets, the modules that handle proposals and votes. Fort Canning replaces all three with a newly introduced set: Referenda, Conviction Voting, Origins, Whitelist and the Enjin Fellowship. Under OpenGov, any account can submit a referendum on one of fifteen tracks, and from the moment the upgrade lands, Matrixchain's own upgrades go through that process.

A track is a lane for a particular kind of decision. Enjin's changelog describes the families: Root and the admin tracks for the highest-stakes changes, treasury tracks sized by how much a proposal would spend, and two special tracks, Referendum Killer and Referendum Canceller, for stopping a proposal that shouldn't proceed. Each track has its own deposit, approval curve and enactment period, and the Enjin Fellowship can fast-track time-sensitive proposals.

Splitting decisions this way means a small treasury request doesn't face the same bar as a change to the chain's core. Riskier tracks demand larger deposits and more support, while smaller ones move faster and cost less.

The submission deposit rises from 0.025 ENJ to 1,000 ENJ on every track, a 40,000-fold increase. The deposit is refunded when a referendum passes or is canceled, and it exists to deter spam. As an illustration, using the roughly $66 million market cap reported in early October, ENJ traded near three cents, which would put 1,000 ENJ around $33.

That is only the entry ticket. The cost that matters comes next. A referendum also needs a decision deposit before it moves into voting, and the changelog lists steep figures: 2,500,000 ENJ on Root and Fellowship Admin, 1,000,000 ENJ on the other admin tracks, and 2,500 to 250,000 ENJ on the treasury tracks. At the same illustrative price, the 2.5 million ENJ Root deposit comes to roughly $80,000, about 0.12% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance.

So proposing is cheap, and pushing a proposal through is not. Anyone can raise an idea, but anyone who wants the network to vote on something big needs real stake in the outcome. The changelog says the same values apply on both chains, and Matrixchain adopts them for its fresh tracks.

According to recent reports, the best evidence of how these votes work comes from the Relaychain referendum that has already finished. Enjin's governance portal shows referendum #16 as finalised, approved on October 28 and enacted on November 9.

Industry observers note that the final tally on the page is small. Eleven voters cast 381,303.02 ENJ of conviction-weighted voting power, and all of it went to Aye: 100% in favor, 0 ENJ against. The page also shows raw, unweighted support of 271,303.2 ENJ, which it describes as the total balance backing the proposal and the figure the support curve uses. The conviction multiplier on the page runs from under 1x up to 6x.

Two numbers stand out. First, an entire chain upgrade passed with 271,303 ENJ of raw support, about 0.013% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance, a figure worked out from the portal's number. Second, conviction added about 110,000 ENJ of weight on top of the raw balance, an average multiplier of roughly 1.4x. Voters picked up some extra weight, but most didn't lock their tokens for the long periods that earn the top multipliers.

Sources indicate that A 100% Aye result states little by itself. A scheduled upgrade with no organized opposition passes easily, and the tally shows how thin engagement was.

Fort Canning adds the safeguard that thin turnout calls for. A referendum now needs a minimum share of total ENJ voting in support. The changelog sets 0.5% on Root and the admin tracks, 0.005% to 0.125% on the treasury tracks, 0.1% for Referendum Killer and 0.05% for Referendum Canceller. Measured against 2.02 billion ENJ, that means about 10.1 million ENJ on Root, roughly 101,000 to 2.5 million on the treasury tracks, about 2.02 million to kill a referendum and about 1.01 million to cancel one.

Recent findings suggest that referendum #16's 271,303 ENJ of raw support would clear the lowest treasury floor of about 101,000 ENJ, but it would miss the Root floor by a factor of about 37. The page doesn't show which track the referendum used, and a runtime upgrade typically sits on a high-stakes track, so the Root comparison works as an illustration and not as a finding. The floors also didn't exist when #16 passed, since Fort Canning introduced them.

That is the real change. Under the new rules, 11 wallets can't carry a chain-level decision on their own. Low turnout means failure, and proposals that matter will need far more ENJ behind them. Enjin's changelog says Matrixchain upgrades go through OpenGov starting with this one, which suggests today's vote still runs on the current system, so the floors will first bite on the first OpenGov referendum.

Industry observers note that holders who haven't voted can still do so through Enjin's governance portal before the window closes. Voting locks tokens, so the lock length is worth checking first. Enjin's support article on voting explains the trade-off: the longer the lock, the more a vote counts, and tokens stay locked until the period ends.

In a recent development, node operators on the Matrixchain can wait for the result before upgrading, as Enjin has indicated, and then follow the changelog for the version to install. Relaychain operators already needed client version 1.8.1.

This vote is more about control than speed. OpenGov spreads decisions across tracks with deposits and support floors built for the weight of each choice, and it moves ENJ holders from voting on a handful of items to a standing governance system. The Relaychain's first vote showed how little participation it took under the old rules, and the first referenda after November 16 will show whether holders turn out for the upcoming ones. If most proposals stall at the decision deposit, the system costs too much. If they clear with a handful of voters, the floors aren't doing their job. Either result will tell holders what their ENJ can do.

Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom: The AI Stock Winners and Losers After Jensen Huang’s Ousting.

Wall Street is picking winners and losers from Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, and the market is treating the chipmaker's competitors considerably better than companies tied to its business.

Nvidia shares fell 4.59% to $165.75 Thursday afternoon, recovering from an opening price of $151.01 and an intraday low of $148.80.

The rebound softened an initial collapse of more than 14%, but the stock remained firmly in negative territory.

The selloff followed Huang's immediate resignation as CEO, president, and board member after reports of extramarital affairs and allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, although the manufacturer has not established that corporate secrets were compromised.

It has been revealed that the stock was already in trouble before Huang stepped down. Nvidia had lost approximately $1.27 trillion in market capitalization between October 6 and November 6, raising questions about AI spending even before the leadership crisis intensified.

AMD climbed 5.79% to $584.89 after opening at $569.28, making it one of the clearest beneficiaries of Thursday's trading.

The manufacturer competes directly with Nvidia in AI accelerators, and uncertainty around Nvidia's leadership could make customers more interested in diversifying their chip suppliers.

Broadcom followed a similar trajectory, gaining 5.65% to $364.73 from an opening price of $356.80.

Unlike AMD, which competes through its own GPU products, Broadcom specializes in custom AI processors and networking technology, offering large customers a different way to reduce their dependence on Nvidia.

Google’s parent manufacturer Alphabet also advanced, rising 2.06% to $299.49 after opening at $293.77.

Google has been expanding its Tensor Processing Unit business, including two fresh AI chip systems unveiled Monday that target privacy-sensitive and memory-intensive workloads.

Those alternatives existed before Huang resigned, and Thursday's gains do not establish that Nvidia has lost customers. Investors may simply be pricing in better competitive opportunities if the leadership transition disrupts Nvidia's strategy or customer relationships.

Nvidia-backed CoreWeave suffered a much rougher session, falling 7.49% to $56.22 after opening at $50.91.

Its decline came just one day after the cloud provider surged 24.7% following quarterly revenue growth of 168%, so this may be just as much a correction after an explosive movement as it is a reaction to Huang’s ousting.

Industry observers note that in any case, the relationship between the companies helps explain the anxiety among investors. Nvidia invested another $2 billion in CoreWeave in January and has an initial $6.3 billion agreement to purchase unused computing capacity through April 2032, making it an investor, supplier, and customer of the same organization.

Any change in Nvidia's investment priorities could therefore affect CoreWeave beyond ordinary chip purchases, although neither company has unveiled changes to those agreements.

The pressure also reached the semiconductor supply chain. TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's advanced processors, fell 1.15% to $408.61 after opening at $394.62, while memory supplier Micron lost 2.70%, trading at $789.43 after opening at $769.31.

SK Hynix, another major supplier of high-bandwidth memory used in AI hardware, declined 3% to $137.98 from an opening price of $134.25.

These companies depend on broader chip demand, however, so their losses cannot be attributed entirely to Nvidia's leadership problems.

For investors, the immediate concern is less about whether AI chips will stop selling and more about how Nvidia manages its partnerships, financing commitments, and product roadmap without the executive who built much of that network.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia's board has said it expects operations and customer commitments to continue without interruption. The manufacturer is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on November 17, with Kress now leading the business through its first earnings announcement since Huang's departure.

The LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has collected 22 of 35 votes (62.86%).

Three more validators have signed on over the past three weeks. Ripple's own nodes have already voted yes, along with the University of Waterloo and UC Berkeley.

To go live, the amendment has to clear the 80% bar (29 votes) and hold it for two straight weeks.

The related SingleAssetVault amendment (XLS-65) has 23 votes (65.7%) and needs six more.

Sources indicate that the XLS-65 and XLS-66 standards drop overcollateralization and instant liquidations and let companies take out fixed-term, uncollateralized loans directly on XRPL. The loans work similarly to traditional bank credit, with a fixed term and pre-set interest terms.

Ripple has already tested the protocol on a private XRPL network with nine nodes that matched the hardware of its mainnet nodes.

Recent findings suggest that holders deposit XRP or stablecoins such as RLUSD into Single Asset Vaults and receive shares. Interest is paid on a cash basis. Depositors receive it only after the borrower has sent the money. Withdrawals from a vault are processed on a first-come, first-served basis.

It has been revealed that borrowers are vetted off-chain by Loan Brokers, who record each disbursement on the ledger. According to the XRPL documentation, the protocol "relies on off-chain underwriting and risk management to assess the creditworthiness of borrowers.".

The broker's own "first-loss capital" covers losses first when a client stops paying.

It has been revealed that issuers can also freeze assets or claw them back. According to Ripple, all operations in a vault and in the connected lending protocol stop when an asset issuer freezes the vault.

Until now, XRP holders who wanted passive income had to use third-party bridges and wrapped tokens. After the amendment activates, holders can deposit XRP in a pool on XRPL, with its fraction-of-a-cent fees, and collect part of the interest paid by borrowers. Their income will depend on the terms set by the loan broker and on borrowers' repayments.

If a major borrower defaults and the broker's first-loss capital runs out, depositors bear the losses and their shares drop in value.

It has been revealed that bitcoin price crashes below the psychologically important $70,000 level for the first time since August, extending a broader crypto market sell-off as a stronger US dollar and rising expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike weigh on investor sentiment. The decline triggered a wave of forced liquidations across derivatives markets, with more than $1.6 billion in leveraged positions wiped out over 24 hours.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin (BTC) dropped as low as $67,770 on November 13, its weakest level since August 19, while Ethereum (ETH) briefly reached $1,900, marking its lowest price since August 18. The CoinDesk 20 Index also declined by 2%, reflecting the broader pressure across digital assets.

In a recent development, macroeconomic developments have become a major source of pressure for cryptocurrency markets. The US Dollar Index climbed above 103, reaching its highest level since April 2025, as traders adjusted their expectations for Federal Reserve policy following hotter-than-expected inflation data.

According to CME FedWatch figures, markets were pricing in an 88% probability of a 25-basis-point rate increase at the Fed’s December meeting. The remaining 12% reflected expectations of a larger, 50-basis-point increase.

It has been revealed that higher interest rates can weigh on assets such as Bitcoin because they make traditional interest-bearing investments more attractive. Rising bond yields and a stronger dollar have therefore added to the challenges facing digital assets.

The market downturn also coincided with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, which sent shares of the technology organization down approximately 4%. Given Bitcoin’s recent correlation with technology stocks, renewed weakness in the sector added another source of selling pressure.

It has been revealed that the speed of Bitcoin’s decline triggered substantial losses among leveraged traders. CoinGlass data showed that approximately $1.64 billion in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, with long positions accounting for nearly 89% of the total.

Sources indicate that bitcoin-related liquidations reached $916 million, including a significant concentration of bullish positions. Longs represented 95.2% of Bitcoin’s forced closures, while Ethereum recorded another $289 million in liquidations, with 89.5% coming from long positions.

The largest individual liquidation involved a Bitcoin long position worth approximately $31.1 million on Hyperliquid.

According to recent reports, derivatives activity also increased sharply during the sell-off. Crypto futures trading volume climbed 58.3% to $269.1 billion, while total open interest declined 4.6% to $120.2 billion. This combination suggests traders were closing positions and reducing exposure as prices moved lower.

Institutional flows have provided another indication of weakening demand. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $47.7 million in net withdrawals on Thursday, extending their losing streak to six consecutive sessions.

Recent findings suggest that the withdrawals brought cumulative outflows over that period to around $1.44 billion, according to data. Continued redemptions from these funds suggest that some investors are reducing their Bitcoin exposure amid the deteriorating market environment.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, traders are turning their attention to upcoming US economic data. October producer price figures are expected later on November 13, with economists forecasting a monthly increase of 0.4%. The Federal Reserve’s next policy meeting is scheduled for December 8–9, keeping interest-rate expectations firmly in focus.

Bitcoin’s break below $70,000 represents a significant deterioration in short-term market sentiment. The recent low near $67,770 is now an crucial level to watch, as another move below it could expose the market to further downside pressure.

A recovery above $70,000, meanwhile, would offer an initial indication that buyers are attempting to regain control. However, persistent ETF withdrawals, elevated liquidation activity, and uncertainty surrounding Federal Reserve policy could make a sustained recovery difficult.

The next direction may depend on whether macroeconomic developments ease pressure on risk assets and whether institutional demand begins to stabilize.

Breaking: Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Sumber: https://decrypt.co/383144/illinois-crypto-tax-draws-alliance-doj-banks-defi

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi.
  • An unusually broad coalition, spanning the U.S.
  • The groups filed briefs this month in Illinois state court supporting a lawsuit from the Crypto Council for Innovation and the Blockchain Association, which are asking a judge to strike down the state’s Digital Asset Tax Act and permanently block its enforcement.

Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi.

An unusually broad coalition, spanning the U.S. Justice Department, Wall Street’s biggest lobby, the national Chamber of Commerce and a who’s-who of crypto firms, has thrown its weight behind a legal challenge to Illinois’ first-of-its-kind tax on digital asset transactions.

The groups filed briefs this month in Illinois state court supporting a lawsuit from the Crypto Council for Innovation and the Blockchain Association, which are asking a judge to strike down the state’s Digital Asset Tax Act and permanently block its enforcement.

The tax imposes a 0.2% levy on the full value of a digital asset every time an Illinois customer trades, transfers, or stores it through a broker, even when there’s no sale, gain, or change in ownership.

Critics have called it among the most punitive crypto taxes in the country, in part because Illinois imposes no comparable tax on dollars, gold, stocks or any other asset, and no other state has anything like it.

On Nov. 6, the Justice Department filed a statement of interest arguing the tax undermines federal policy and U.S. leadership in digital assets, calling it vague and discriminatory for singling out crypto for treatment no other asset faces.

It has been revealed that the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, which represents hundreds of broker-dealers, banks and asset managers, filed an amicus brief warning the tax reaches well beyond crypto-native platforms to the traditional banks, custodians and advisers increasingly offering digital asset products.

A separate brief filed Nov. 11 brought together crypto’s heavy hitters, led by the DeFi Education Fund, Andreessen Horowitz, Paradigm and Uniswap, and including Aave Labs, Chainlink Labs, Solana Policy Institute, Phantom, Jito Labs, Multicoin Capital and Stand With Crypto.

Sources indicate that their filing argues the law’s definitions are so vague they could stretch to software developers and decentralized protocols that hold no customer funds and have no way to identify consumers or know where a transaction occurred. The brief noted an estimated 2.64 million Illinoisans hold digital assets, the fifth-highest total of any state.

“This tax is unclear, discriminatory, unconstitutional, and harmful to the future of finance,” CCI CEO Ji Hun Kim and Blockchain Association executive Ashok Pinto said in a joint statement.

The challenge dates to August. As Decrypt reported, Illinois agreed in October to pause the tax until July 1, 2027, buying time for the court fight now underway.

Strategy shares declined Thursday following MSCI’s decision to remove the organization from its indexes, as Bitcoin also fell amid a broader crypto market decline.

Shares of Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin treasury tech giant Strategy fell 6.49% on Thursday, closing at $114.41, a day after MSCI confirmed the company’s removal from its global equity indexes and amid a broader cryptocurrency market sell-off.

Recent findings suggest that on Wednesday, MSCI confirmed that Strategy would be removed from its global equity indexes after the Nov. 30 market close, a move that could trigger selling by funds tracking the benchmarks. JPMorgan previously estimated that the exclusion could result in roughly $2.8 billion in selling pressure.

Ryan Kirkley, CEO of Global Settlement Network, told Cointelegraph that MSCI’s decision could help distinguish Bitcoin treasury companies from traditional operating businesses and limit indirect cryptocurrency exposure for passive investors.

“Index inclusion meant ordinary passive investors, like someone holding a global index fund in their pension, were getting leveraged Bitcoin exposure they never chose. MSCI just fixed that,” he said.

Kirkley added that MSCI’s decision also raises broader questions about whether Bitcoin treasury companies should be classified alongside traditional operating businesses.

Sources indicate that in its Aug. 31 response to MSCI’s proposed rules, Strategy argued that the changes were a pretext for targeting digital asset treasury companies. It also downplayed the potential financial impact, saying MSCI-linked funds held approximately 13 million of its shares, representing just 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding.

The stock’s decline coincided with a broader cryptocurrency market sell-off. Bitcoin traded near $71,340 as of 4:08 p.m. ET on Thursday, down 4.3% over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko data. The total cryptocurrency market capitalization declined 3% to around $2.49 trillion.

#269. US Justice Department, business groups and DeFi firms challenge Illinois crypto tax

US Justice Department, business groups and DeFi firms challenge Illinois crypto tax

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://cointelegraph.com/news/us-justice-department-business-groups-defi-illinois-crypto-tax?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry groups argued in court filings that Illinois’ crypto tax, which applies even when a transaction yields no profit, could raise compliance costs and violate federal law.
  • The US Department of Justice, business and financial industry groups and a coalition of decentralized finance (DeFi) firms have backed a legal challenge to Illinois’ 0.2% digital asset tax, arguing that the measure unfairly targets cryptocurrency transactions and could impose taxes even when investors make no profit.
  • Industry observers note that over the past week, the Justice Department filed a statement of interest, while the US Chamber of Commerce and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (SIFMA) submitted an amicus filing.

Industry groups argued in court filings that Illinois’ crypto tax, which applies even when a transaction yields no profit, could raise compliance costs and violate federal law.

The US Department of Justice, business and financial industry groups and a coalition of decentralized finance (DeFi) firms have backed a legal challenge to Illinois’ 0.2% digital asset tax, arguing that the measure unfairly targets cryptocurrency transactions and could impose taxes even when investors make no profit.

Industry observers note that over the past week, the Justice Department filed a statement of interest, while the US Chamber of Commerce and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (SIFMA) submitted an amicus filing. A coalition that includes venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Paradigm as well as crypto protocols Uniswap and Aave Labs also filed a brief, according to a Thursday announcement from the Blockchain Association and Crypto Council for Innovation.

The law, enacted in June, imposes a 0.2% tax on the value of digital assets exchanged, transferred or stored, regardless of whether a transaction generates a profit.

The Digital Chamber sued Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and state revenue official David Harris in July, followed by a separate challenge from the Blockchain Association and Crypto Council for Innovation in August. Originally scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, the tax was delayed until July 1, 2027, allowing more time for the legal challenges.

In a recent development, illinois had projected the digital asset tax would generate $60 million in fiscal year 2027 revenue, according to estimates from the governor’s budget office. Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch previously promoted the measure as part of a broader affordability agenda aimed at “closing corporate loopholes and making significant tech companies and crypto billionaires pay their fair share,” the Chicago Tribune reported in July.

Lawmakers involved in advancing the legislation and the governor’s office did not respond to Cointelegraph’s requests for comment before publication.

Related: France advances stablecoin tax, eyes self-custodial wallets and exit tax proposals.

In a Nov. 6 court filing, SIFMA and the US Chamber of Commerce warned that Illinois’ tax would affect banks, broker-dealers, custodians and asset managers across the country, potentially exposing them to significant compliance costs. They also highlighted the financial burden on customers.

“This means that a customer who loses money owes the same tax as a customer who earns a profit,” the filing mentioned. “And a customer who moves the same asset between two accounts faces tax (potentially on both ends) without a sale, a gain, or a change in beneficial ownership.”.

The groups said firms would need to develop systems to identify Illinois customers, value digital assets and determine which transactions are taxable, while facing potential criminal penalties for violations.

They also argued that the tax discriminates against digital asset services because comparable transactions involving traditional assets are not taxed in the same way, potentially violating federal internet tax protections and constitutional requirements for interstate commerce and uniform taxation.

The Justice Department also weighed in on Nov. 6, saying that Illinois’ digital asset tax undermines federal efforts to promote cryptocurrency innovation and US leadership in the sector.

In a recent development, the filing cited the creation of a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and the GENIUS Act, which established federal rules for stablecoins. The DOJ argued that less favorable tax treatment for digital assets could conflict with those policies.

Industry observers note that separately, the DeFi coalition warned about who could be held responsible for collecting the tax. In a Nov. 11 filing, the group argued that Illinois’ proposed rules could impose obligations on software developers and other blockchain participants who lack customer information, control over user funds or the ability to collect taxes.

#270. Tech Report: Solana Moves Closer To Wall Street As DTCC Reveals Tokenization Looks

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words)
General

Tech Report: Solana Moves Closer To Wall Street As DTCC Reveals Tokenization Looks

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/solana-moves-closer-to-wall-street-as-dtcc-reveals-tokenization-plans/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Solana is moving closer to traditional financial markets following a major announcement from the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC).
  • As institutional interest in Solana continues expanding, the Wall Street infrastructure giant has revealed prepares to connect its tokenization service to the blockchain, potentially bringing regulated securities onto the network in 2027.
  • The announcement, published on November 12, marks another significant development in the growing relationship between cryptocurrency infrastructure and traditional finance.

Solana is moving closer to traditional financial markets following a major announcement from the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC).

As institutional interest in Solana continues expanding, the Wall Street infrastructure giant has revealed prepares to connect its tokenization service to the blockchain, potentially bringing regulated securities onto the network in 2027.

The announcement, published on November 12, marks another significant development in the growing relationship between cryptocurrency infrastructure and traditional finance.

DTCC aims to make eligible assets held by its subsidiary, The Depository Trust Company (DTC), available in tokenized form on Solana during the second half of 2027.

For Solana, the development could strengthen its position in the emerging market for tokenized real-world assets.

According to the official DTCC announcement, the tech giant intends to integrate Solana into its existing Tokenization Service.

The service rolled out on October 28, enabling eligible securities held at DTC to be represented digitally while maintaining the ownership rights and investor protections associated with traditional financial assets.

Its planned expansion to Solana could allow participating institutions to convert eligible securities into blockchain-based representations and manage their lifecycle through the network.

The announcement is particularly notable because DTCC operates at the center of the US financial system.

In 2025, its subsidiaries processed securities transactions valued at approximately $4.7 quadrillion, while DTC provided custody and asset servicing for securities valued at $114 trillion.

These figures demonstrate the scale of DTCC’s existing operations, although they do not represent assets committed to Solana.

Frank La Salla, DTCC’s president and CEO, described the initiative as an effort to expand institutional access to regulated tokenized assets while preserving established market protections.

Meanwhile, Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services, emphasized that tokenized securities available through the service would retain their existing ownership rights and regulatory safeguards.

The integration is expected in the second half of 2027, meaning the announcement represents a future expansion rather than an immediate transfer of Wall Street securities onto Solana.

Tokenization allows traditional assets, including eligible stocks, exchange-traded funds, and government securities, to be represented on blockchain networks.

Supporters believe this technology could improve settlement efficiency, simplify collateral transfers, and enable more flexible asset management.

For Solana, attracting regulated financial infrastructure could be an important step toward broader institutional adoption.

The blockchain is already known for relatively low transaction costs and fast processing, characteristics that could support applications requiring frequent asset transfers.

The Solana Foundation has also emphasized the network’s growing role in institutional finance.

Nick Ducoff, the foundation’s general manager of institutional business, said the planned DTCC connection would bring established financial infrastructure closer to an ecosystem already supporting real-world financial activity.

We believe the most crucial development is not simply the possibility of additional tokenized assets, but the credibility that participation by a major financial infrastructure provider could bring to Solana.

This could encourage more financial institutions to examine the network for settlement, collateral management, and tokenized investment products.

However, the potential implications for SOL’s price require careful consideration.

Although transactions on Solana generally use SOL for network fees, greater tokenized asset activity does not automatically translate into a proportional increase in demand for the cryptocurrency.

Institutional adoption would need to generate sustained network activity, liquidity, and demand for SOL to create a meaningful longer-term market effect.

The real-world asset market has become an increasingly notable area of blockchain development.

Rather than focusing exclusively on cryptocurrency trading, financial institutions are exploring how blockchain infrastructure can support traditional investment products.

DTCC’s tokenization service could eventually connect these two markets more directly.

In a recent development, the service initially launched with integrations involving the Canton Network and DTCC’s private Besu network. Adding Solana would expand the range of blockchain environments available to eligible participants.

This multi-network strategy is vital because it suggests institutions may prefer interoperability rather than relying on a single blockchain.

Solana could benefit from being included among the networks selected to support regulated financial activity.

Nevertheless, several questions remain unanswered.

DTCC has not disclosed how much value could eventually be tokenized on Solana, which institutions will use the integration, or the exact securities that will become available.

Participation will also remain subject to the service’s regulatory and operational requirements.

For investors following Solana ecosystem growth, these details will be vital indicators of whether the announcement translates into measurable adoption.

The next milestones will include technical integration progress, announcements from participating institutions, and the eventual availability of eligible tokenized assets.

While the integration remains scheduled for 2027, the announcement reinforces a broader trend: major financial infrastructure providers are increasingly exploring public blockchain networks.

For Solana, that could prove more important over the long term than any immediate reaction in SOL’s price.

#271. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9 min read (1745 words)
AI & Tech

How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Sumber: https://nulltx.com/how-bittensors-gamma-turns-every-ai-payment-into-an-alpha-burn

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token.
  • Sources indicate that using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine.
  • According to recent reports, customers have two ways in.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Sources indicate that using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor declared gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

According to recent reports, customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Owners who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

The gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

Gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example demonstrates the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

Recent findings suggest that to use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

In a recent development, the limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is confirmed, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

Recent findings suggest that the docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

Industry observers note that that makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit.

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake.

According to recent reports, on Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee.

In a recent development, huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government.

But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go.

According to recent reports, the market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The tech giant that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list.

Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a firm built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him?

Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed, writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the tech giant he built.

It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.

— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) November 12, 2026.

Sources indicate that erik Voorhees, who founded ShapeShift and privacy-focused AI platform Venice, was more confrontational. “The entire coup against Jensen Huang can be halted by asking a single question,” he wrote. “What evidence is there that Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy? The answer, unsurprisingly, is absolutely zero.”.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia notes it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities remarked they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang.

Sources indicate that anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote. “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.”.

Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.

— Anthony Pompliano 🌪 (@APompliano) November 12, 2026.

Industry observers note that surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat.

For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked, alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform.

That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.”.

Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them.

The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services.

Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.”.

OpenAI and Anthropic have spent millions lobbying the US Congress to ban open weights.

When they formed the "Pace the Frontier" group to push for strict limits on open models, Jensen stepped up right away.

He created the Open Secure Alliance to fight back.

Look at the list of… pic.twitter.com/OeasotcLO3.

In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance, which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions.

The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang.

OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his manufacturer had never advocated such a ban.

Industry observers note that other posts on social media showed how much anxiety the debate had generated. A commenter replied to Song that they were now “counting on Huawei and Deepseek for the very survival of the OSS community.”.

Huawei and Deepseek are two major Chinese companies, known for their open-source developments.

I can't believe now I am counting on Huawei and Deepseek for the very survival of the OSS community. What a loss...

— Look4Newways (@sflk2026) November 12, 2026.

Sources indicate that the issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027.

That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence—arguably, the most powerful company on earth.

Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote, praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous manufacturer.

Sources indicate that A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity. Jensen founded and ran one of the few companies to reach a massive scale while driving massive continued innovation and ubiquity, while others fell into the trap of ever-increasing extraction. https://t.co/AkS5XT9HF8.

— Tim Sweeney (@TimSweeneyEpic) November 12, 2026.

Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote. He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI.

Industry observers note that peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X. “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.”.

If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.

— Peter Steinberger (@steipete) November 12, 2026.

According to recent reports, financial commentator The Kobeissi Letter had urged the board to consult shareholders before any decision, arguing that there was no obvious replacement and citing research on the costs of ousting successful CEOs. After the announcement, the account called the resignation “the most costly mistake of the AI Revolution.”.

Former DWS executive and corporate-governance critic Desiree Fixler invoked directors’ fiduciary duty, saying the board should protect shareholders instead of indulging what she called a media frenzy.

Industry observers note that in general, most of the reactions were supportive, separating personal affairs from business. The corporate espionage angle has apparently not swayed tech enthusiasts.

Bitcoin and privacy advocate Neil Woodfine described Huang as a founder who had built Nvidia to the pinnacle and championed free, local AI, only to be displaced by a managerial establishment convinced it could do better.

This Jensen Huang thing is so ugly. Guy takes a company from zero to absolute pinnacle, through blood, sweat, and tears, a pure founder’s founder, great products, makes so many people rich beyond their imaginations, champions open free local AI, and then the incumbent modern….

— Neil Woodfine (@nwoodfine) November 12, 2026.

Industry observers note that not everyone outside that chorus thought the security questions could be set aside. North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer had called for Huang’s exit, warning about the risk of blackmail and saying the internal investigation was insufficient. The concern from Washington has been largely uniform: the possibility of compromising pressure against the leader of a tech giant central to U.S. AI infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, President Donald Trump has remained supportive of Huang: “He’s definitely suffering,” he told the press. “I think he’ll be in good shape.”.

Sources indicate that speculation about Huang’s next job spread just as promptly as criticism of his last one. Responding to an X user asking him to hire Huang, Elon Musk replied, “That would be an honor.”.

Nvidia says its board is searching for a permanent CEO from inside and outside the company, with Kress running the business in the meantime. Its next scheduled earnings report is November 17, the first major financial update investors will receive after Huang’s departure.

#275. DTCC Intends Solana Expansion as Wallet Rules Limit Access

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words)
General

DTCC Intends Solana Expansion as Wallet Rules Limit Access

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://cointelegraph.com/news/dtcc-plans-solana-expansion-wallet-rules-limit-access?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US securities clearinghouse looks to bring tokenized stocks to Solana in 2027, but analysts say restrictions could limit adoption.
  • Intends by the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation’s (DTCC) to bring tokenized securities to Solana could attract more traditional financial institutions to the blockchain, but regulatory restrictions may limit the impact on the network, according to analysts.
  • DTCC revealed Thursday that it plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027.

The US securities clearinghouse looks to bring tokenized stocks to Solana in 2027, but analysts say restrictions could limit adoption.

Intends by the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation’s (DTCC) to bring tokenized securities to Solana could attract more traditional financial institutions to the blockchain, but regulatory restrictions may limit the impact on the network, according to analysts.

DTCC revealed Thursday that it plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027. The move would allow certain securities held by its Depository Trust Organization (DTC) subsidiary to be turned into digital tokens on the network.

Solana is a blockchain known for its fast transactions and low fees, making it popular for crypto trading, especially memecoins. The network had about $4.94 billion in total value locked (TVL) as of Nov. 12, according to DefiLlama.

In a recent development, experts say the move could help Solana attract more activity beyond just memecoins, but it’s not clear how much fresh capital and transaction volume it could bring to the network. What’s more, current US regulatory rules still limit who can hold and transfer the tokenized assets.

Alex Lin, founding partner at venture capital firm Reforge, noted Solana’s history of handling large amounts of memecoin trading may have helped show that the network can support traditional financial activity.

Recent findings suggest that “Memes were a public stress test that gave Solana credibility that it can handle retail-scale volume cheaply and reliably,” Lin told Cointelegraph. “The casino paved the way for more institutional plumbing.”.

Sources indicate that however, under a December 2025 SEC no-action letter, DTC participants must register wallets to hold tokenized securities. The tokens can only be transferred between registered wallets, potentially limiting usage.

It has been revealed that “It’s overstated in the near term because the SEC relief from Dec 2025 keeps these tokens in a walled garden of registered DTC participants, so permissionless retail and DeFi liquidity can’t touch these tokens directly yet,” Lin stated. “Regulators need to let these assets work as true onchain collateral and that’s more policy than tech.”.

DTCC launched its tokenization service on the Canton Network and its private Besu network on Oct. 28, allowing certain securities to be turned into digital tokens while keeping the same investor protections. At launch, DTCC remarked 20 DTC participants had signed agreements to access the service, but it has not said whether any plan to use Solana.

Cointelegraph contacted DTCC and the Solana Foundation for additional comments but has not yet heard back.

Related: Robinhood’s Tenev warns US tokenization uncertainty deters ‘serious assets’.

Kha Nguyen, CEO and co-founder of blockchain analytics platform Birdeye, which tracks trading activity on Solana, stated the blockchain has already seen growing demand for tokenized stocks without DTCC’s involvement.

According to Birdeye’s H1 2026 report, tokenized-stock trading volume on Solana reached around $4.9 billion in the first half of the year, more than six times the volume recorded in the previous six months.

Birdeye’s third-quarter report also found that more than 1 million accounts held tokenized stocks on Solana by late September.

Still, broader trading activity on Solana has slowed with the network recording about 6.9 billion transactions in the 30 days ending Nov. 11, down almost 40% from the previous 30-day period, according to Token Terminal data. Meanwhile, trading volume on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) fell 34.4% to $39.1 billion, while monthly active addresses dropped nearly 13% to 45.8 million.

Industry observers note that network fees also fell 39% to about $17 million over the same period. However, the value of tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) on Solana rose almost 7% to $4.76 billion as of Nov. 11 – up from $4.46 billion on Oct. 12.

“By late September more than a million wallets had held a tokenized stock, and real-world assets on Solana had grown five times in a year,” Nguyen told Cointelegraph.

Nguyen remarked bringing more tokenized securities onto the network does not automatically mean more transactions or greater demand for Solana’s native cryptocurrency, SOL. “A trade is one transaction whether it moves $100 or $100 million,” Nguyen said. “What matters is turnover, not value parked on-chain.”.

In a recent development, nguyen noted DTCC’s integration would need support from banks and other financial firms to have a real impact on Solana. Institutions would also need enough liquidity to support large trades.

“Banks, brokers and issuers need to say they will problem, trade and settle there, and then do it,” Nguyen noted. He added that institutions would need to actively use the tokenized securities rather than simply hold them.

“The assets must be active, not idle: traded around the clock, used as collateral to borrow against, and earning yield,” Nguyen noted.

Lin agreed that the longer-term impact would depend on how the assets are used, rather than which blockchain they are issued on.

“No one cares where the assets are issued, but more so where they’re used,” Lin noted. “It’s all about where secondary trading and collateral activity will happen and ultimately settle.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

Ripple-backed XRP treasury tech giant Evernorth Holdings (XRPN) is under extreme pressure as its shares have declined by over 40% while substantial investors like Ripple Labs move closer to potentially selling millions of shares.

Sources indicate that earlier this week, Evernorth filed a prospectus with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), indicating that the XRP-focused manufacturer has registered a whopping 73,688,162 Class A shares for potential resale by existing shareholders.

Evernorth's prospectus comes as the XRP-focused tech giant is enduring a brutal stock market debut. XRPN began trading on Nasdaq on Oct. 12.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 10, Evernorth's stock price dropped 23.54%. XRPN ended the day at $7.96, compared to $10.41 in the previous trading session. Moreover, about 1.39 million shares were traded, which is a significant jump from about 369,000 shares on Nov. 9.

So far, Evernorth's share price has declined by around 48% from its closing price on Oct. 28 ($15.26). The magnitude of the decline is even greater if we consider the high share price on its debut day ($19.39). XRPN's stock price is down by around 59% from that high.

Some of the biggest names and companies linked to the XRP ecosystem are shareholders who have registered shares for potential sale, as per the prospectus filed with the SEC.

For instance, the biggest shareholder is Arrington XRP Capital Fund, which was a sponsor of the merger between Evernorth and Armada Acquisition Corp. II. It has about 33.82 million shares registered for possible resale.

Similarly, the second-largest shareholder is Ripple Labs, which has about 18.14 million shares registered. Then there are various entities linked to SBI Holdings, a big Japanese financial institution. They have 11.79 million shares registered, as per the prospectus filed with the SEC.

The Larsen Lam Children's Remainder Trust, which is linked to Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen, has about 7.15 million shares registered for possible sale.

Other names mentioned in the filing include Pantera Capital, GSR Markets Switzerland and Kraken parent firm Payward.

It is important to understand that the fact that they've registered shares for sale doesn't mean that these investors have sold their holdings or necessarily plan to sell them.

For example, Ripple, the Arrington-sponsored entity and a Larsen-linked entity are all subject to six-month lock-up agreements following the completion of Evernorth's business combination on Oct. 9.

These lock-up agreements are typically set to expire on April 9, 2027, with some exceptions.

#279. Bitcoin Enters The AI Economy As Lightning Labs Releases Payments For Autonomous Agents

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words)
AI & Tech

Bitcoin Enters The AI Economy As Lightning Labs Releases Payments For Autonomous Agents

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/bitcoin-enters-the-ai-economy-as-lightning-labs-launches-payments-for-autonomous-agents/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin could be entering a latest phase of adoption as artificial intelligence developers explore ways for autonomous software to make payments without human intervention.
  • While Bitcoin’s Lightning Network has traditionally focused on faster and cheaper transactions, Lightning Labs has introduced a latest technology called pi402 that allows AI coding agents to purchase computing services directly using BTC.
  • Declared on November 12, the open-source technology enables AI agents to pay for the computing power required to generate responses, analyze information, and perform other tasks.

Bitcoin could be entering a latest phase of adoption as artificial intelligence developers explore ways for autonomous software to make payments without human intervention.

While Bitcoin’s Lightning Network has traditionally focused on faster and cheaper transactions, Lightning Labs has introduced a latest technology called pi402 that allows AI coding agents to purchase computing services directly using BTC.

Declared on November 12, the open-source technology enables AI agents to pay for the computing power required to generate responses, analyze information, and perform other tasks.

The development could introduce a new source of Bitcoin payment activity as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into everyday digital services.

According to the official Lightning Labs announcement, pi402 allows AI coding agents to pay for inference directly through Bitcoin’s Lightning Network.

Inference refers to the computing process that occurs when an artificial intelligence model generates an answer or completes a task.

Traditionally, developers access these services through subscriptions, prepaid credits, or accounts linked to credit cards.

However, Lightning Labs believes this payment structure creates unnecessary obstacles for autonomous software.

With pi402, an AI agent can request access to a paid service, receive a payment invoice, complete the transaction using Bitcoin, and continue its work without requiring a person to approve each purchase.

The system uses Lightning’s L402 payment authentication protocol, which combines payment verification with access to digital services.

Once the payment is completed, the agent receives the credentials needed to access the requested computing resources.

The process can happen within seconds, potentially allowing AI applications to make numerous small transactions without relying on traditional banking infrastructure.

Lightning Labs also introduced usage-based billing capabilities, enabling service providers to charge for individual AI tokens rather than requiring customers to purchase large packages in advance.

The technology builds on earlier efforts to expand Bitcoin payment applications beyond conventional cryptocurrency transfers.

The most interesting implication of pi402 is the possibility that autonomous AI agents could become a new category of Bitcoin users.

As artificial intelligence applications become more sophisticated, software agents may increasingly need to purchase data, computing power, and access to other digital services.

Rather than requiring a traditional bank account, these agents could use Bitcoin wallets to complete payments automatically.

This could make the Lightning Network particularly attractive for micropayments.

Unlike conventional card-based payment systems, where fixed processing fees can make very small transactions uneconomical, Lightning supports payments denominated in tiny fractions of Bitcoin.

Lightning Labs explained that its technology can meter AI inference in millisatoshis, with one millisatoshi representing one-thousandth of a satoshi.

This level of precision allows developers to charge for extremely small units of computing activity.

From an investment perspective, growing payment activity could strengthen Bitcoin’s role as an internet-native financial network.

However, increased Lightning transactions would not automatically translate into higher BTC prices.

The longer-term market effect would depend on adoption, the amount of Bitcoin held in payment wallets, and whether demand for BTC grows alongside the services being purchased.

Nevertheless, the development introduces another potential use case at a time when institutional interest in Bitcoin adoption continues expanding.

Artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency have often been discussed as separate technology sectors.

However, autonomous payments could create an vital connection between them.

AI agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks, but paying for services remains a challenge because traditional financial systems generally require human identities, account registration, and payment authorization.

Bitcoin’s Lightning Network offers a different approach.

By allowing software to hold limited balances and complete transactions programmatically, developers can create applications that pay for services as they are needed.

The pi402 extension also supports spending controls, including per-request limits and daily budgets, helping developers restrict how much an agent can spend.

Lightning Labs has made the technology open source, allowing developers to experiment with newly introduced payment applications.

Widespread adoption would require more AI service providers to accept Lightning payments, while developers would need to address wallet security, liquidity management, and the volatility associated with Bitcoin.

Even so, the announcement represents another step toward integrating Bitcoin into emerging digital infrastructure.

For now, pi402 is a newly introduced developer tool rather than evidence of widespread commercial adoption.

But if autonomous AI agents eventually become major consumers of computing services, Bitcoin could find an increasingly important role in how those machines exchange value.

And that could strengthen its long-term utility far beyond the cryptocurrency trading market.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tron, Tether and Chainalysis Form a Fresh Crypto-Crime Task Force—Replacing One That Just Collapsed.
  • Tron, Tether, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis have launched a joint effort to hunt down and disrupt criminal activity involving the USDT stablecoin, just weeks after a nearly identical alliance, with a different analytics partner, quietly fell apart.
  • Confirmed Wednesday, the Digital Crime Task Force aims to identify illicit activity involving Tether’s USDT on the Tron blockchain and surface it for law enforcement before criminals can move their funds.

Tron, Tether and Chainalysis Form a Fresh Crypto-Crime Task Force—Replacing One That Just Collapsed.

Tron, Tether, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis have launched a joint effort to hunt down and disrupt criminal activity involving the USDT stablecoin, just weeks after a nearly identical alliance, with a different analytics partner, quietly fell apart.

Confirmed Wednesday, the Digital Crime Task Force aims to identify illicit activity involving Tether’s USDT on the Tron blockchain and surface it for law enforcement before criminals can move their funds.

The pitch is a shift from reactive to proactive: rather than waiting for a victim to report a crime or an investigator to flag tainted funds, the group says it will proactively trace criminal networks and coordinate asset freezes, drawing on Chainalysis’s intelligence and AI-powered investigative tools. It will also accept tips and freeze requests from police.

“Criminals are using AI to move faster than ever, and waiting for a victim to report a crime is no longer good enough,” noted Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino, noting the company has frozen more than $7 billion tied to illicit activity while working with over 360 law enforcement agencies across 73 countries.

Tron founder Justin Sun framed it as protecting the millions who rely on USDT, which circulates on Tron to the tune of more than $94 billion.

Sources indicate that the notable wrinkle is what this fresh alliance replaces. Tron and Tether previously ran a similar operation, the T3 Financial Crime Unit, formed in 2024 with rival analytics firm TRM Labs and later joined by Binance. Together, the group froze more than $450 million in tainted assets.

Recent findings suggest that but Bloomberg reported earlier this month that T3 was quietly disbanded in late August, with people familiar citing slow response times and a lack of coordination among its members. Its collapse went public just days before the record $6.4 billion Binance hack.

Swapping TRM for Chainalysis is a pointed move, given the two are fierce competitors. Chainalysis has even sued the U.S. government over an ICE contract awarded to TRM without competitive bidding, underscoring the rivalry now running through crypto’s crime-fighting infrastructure.

The upcoming task force says it will target a broad sweep of threats, from romance and investment scams to stolen funds, terrorist financing, North Korean cyber operations, cartel money laundering and child-exploitation material.

The group also framed the effort around a coming era of autonomous AI agents transacting onchain, which it warned will open fresh avenues for criminal exploitation.

#281. Bitcoin Core Breaks Silence on Three Patched Security Vulnerabilities

Bitcoin Core Breaks Silence on Three Patched Security Vulnerabilities

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Sumber: https://u.today/bitcoin-core-breaks-silence-on-three-patched-security-vulnerabilities

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin Core developers have revealed three key security vulnerabilities, including a high-severity flaw that could potentially disrupt the mining capabilities of the Bitcoin network, preventing miners from creating new blocks.
  • Industry observers note that as revealed in security advisories published on Nov.
  • One of the vulnerabilities, titled CVE-2025-62861, was rated as a high-severity glitch due to its potential effect on Bitcoin miners.

Bitcoin Core developers have revealed three key security vulnerabilities, including a high-severity flaw that could potentially disrupt the mining capabilities of the Bitcoin network, preventing miners from creating new blocks.

Industry observers note that as revealed in security advisories published on Nov. 10, the vulnerabilities impacted various elements of the Bitcoin Core software that powers many nodes underpinning the world's leading cryptocurrency.

One of the vulnerabilities, titled CVE-2025-62861, was rated as a high-severity glitch due to its potential effect on Bitcoin miners.

The bug has the potential to create problems after a blockchain reorganization, which is when previously accepted blocks are replaced by the network with an alternative chain.

More precisely, the problem could cause an inconsistent state in the node's mempool, where all unconfirmed transactions are stored.

The vulnerability impacted Bitcoin Core software versions 28.0-28.2 and 29.0-29.1.

Sources indicate that it was first reported on Sept. 26, 2025, by security researcher Niklas Goegge.

Beyond the mining vulnerability, Bitcoin Core developers have revealed two further security problems, rated medium severity.

The first one (CVE-2025-62859) could enable malicious network participants to slow down Bitcoin block processing through an exploit that involves changes in transaction witness data.

Under some circumstances, it could make an affected node wait for up to 10 minutes before processing a block.

Moreover, such an attack could be repeated indefinitely on the node when the latter is running in specific configurations.

The vulnerability was found by Eugene Siegel in April 2025.

The second vulnerability (CVE-2025-62860) involved Bitcoin nodes that operate on the anonymous Tor network.

In fact, the Bitcoin Core developers revealed that thousands of reachable Bitcoin mainnet nodes had been granting permissions for incoming Tor connections.

Nevertheless, the concern did not affect nodes that do not use the optional whitelist configuration.

The three vulnerabilities are not new discoveries.

In fact, all of the issues were already fixed by the Bitcoin Core developers in October 2025.

It has been revealed that the fixes were integrated into both Bitcoin Core 30.0, which was released on Oct. 10, and Bitcoin Core 29.2, rolled out on Oct. 14.

The high-severity mining vulnerability was also patched in Bitcoin Core 28.3.

The delay in the disclosure of the vulnerabilities was in line with the Bitcoin Core security policy, which usually calls for developers to wait at least two weeks after the end of life of the last affected software version before publishing details of medium- or high-severity vulnerabilities.
